How to Build Your Own Custom AI Jarvis Agent in 9 Steps
items.hook: Learn how to assemble a fully personalized AI assistant that manages your tools and talks back without training your own model.
items.summary: Building your own AI Jarvis doesn't require training a custom AI model from scratch; it's about connecting the right open-source and modular tools. By giving an AI agent a dedicated home server, an agent harness, and persistent long-term memory, you create a system that truly understands your preferences and workflow. You can equip it with specific skills, wire it to your everyday apps like email and calendar, and enable voice communication using realistic text-to-speech. Finally, design a slick custom interface to bring the full movie-style assistant experience to life.

sections.heading: Overview: Modular AI Assembly
sections.detail: Instead of training a custom LLM, build an AI assistant by connecting modular components: hosting, an agent framework, brain model, context, memory, skills, tools, channels, and a frontend interface.

sections.heading: Step 1: Give It a Home
sections.detail: Host your agent on hardware that stays powered on 24/7, such as an old laptop, a Mac mini, or a cheap cloud server.

sections.heading: Step 2: Agent Harness
sections.detail: Use Hermes Agent by Nous Research (a free, open-source framework) to turn raw model outputs into actionable agent behavior.

sections.heading: Step 3: Pick the Brain
sections.detail: Select an LLM model like Claude, OpenAI Codex, or Gemini. Since the framework is modular, you can swap the underlying model at any time.

sections.heading: Step 4: Teach It Who You Are
sections.detail: Provide system prompt context regarding your job, personal goals, and work preferences so responses are tailored specifically to you.

sections.heading: Step 5: Long-Term Memory
sections.detail: Integrate a persistent memory layer using Honcho so the agent retains context and learns from past chat conversations.

sections.heading: Step 6: Add Skills
sections.detail: Equip the agent with specialized skill modules designed to execute specific routine tasks.

sections.heading: Step 7: Connect Your Tools
sections.detail: Connect the agent to daily productivity software, including email, calendar, documents, and web browser automation.

sections.heading: Step 8: Connect Channels & Voice
sections.detail: Link communication channels like Slack, Telegram, or iMessage, and synthesize spoken responses using an ElevenLabs voice (a British accent mimics the iconic Marvel Jarvis).

sections.heading: Step 9: Design the Jarvis Look
sections.detail: Create a visual UI using Claude Design, then write custom code to wire up the audio response stream and interface logic.

followup.answer_html:
What checked out, and what needed fixing

  • Hermes Agent and Honcho are both real. The two links already on this post are their genuine official pages, confirmed by fetching them directly. No links needed to come off the list.
  • "OpenAI Codex" is not a separate brain you can swap in alongside Claude and Gemini. Codex is OpenAI's coding-agent product (app, CLI, IDE extension); the model actually running underneath it is a GPT model (currently gpt-5.3-codex). If you want an OpenAI option, you're picking a GPT model, not "Codex."
  • The ElevenLabs free tier cannot be used commercially and is capped around 10,000 characters a month (roughly 5-10 minutes of speech). ElevenLabs is also retiring its current Default voice library, British voices included, by December 31, 2026, so whatever voice you pick now will likely need replacing.
  • Claude Design is real and current, but it needs a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise). It is not on the free tier, which the reel doesn't mention.
  • Honcho's self-hosted version is genuinely free (AGPL-3.0). The managed cloud version is paid per use (ingestion $2 per million tokens, chat queries $0.001-$0.50 depending on reasoning depth). No official free-credit amount could be confirmed; a "$100 free credit" claim floating online is unverified.
  • Apple has no iMessage API at all. Any bridge, including the one built into Hermes Agent, means running a spare Mac 24/7 signed into your Apple ID, with full disk access granted to the bridge app.

Build order

Phase 1: Backbone (start here)

  1. Home - any machine that stays on: old laptop, Mac mini, or a small cloud server. No product to verify here.
  2. Harness: Hermes Agent - real, MIT license, free and open source, self-hosted, releases landing most weeks. Install with curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash (Linux/macOS/WSL2) or iex (irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1) (Windows PowerShell), then run hermes model to pick a provider. See the quickstart.
  3. Memory: Honcho - real, AGPL-3.0, free if self-hosted (honcho start or Docker). The hosted version is paid per token/query. See the GitHub repo for the quickstart.

Phase 2: Brain

  1. Pick a model - Claude, a GPT model, or Gemini all work as the brain; all are paid APIs. Gemini's Flash-class models have a free tier in Google AI Studio; Gemini Pro, Claude and GPT models do not have a standing free tier. Swapping between them is a matter of an API key in Hermes Agent (hermes model). Claude pricing, OpenAI pricing, Gemini pricing.
  2. You and 6. Skills - no product here to verify. Write a short system prompt covering your work, goals and preferences, then add task-specific skill modules in Hermes Agent's own format.

Phase 3: Voice and interface

8 (voice half). ElevenLabs - real. Free tier exists (10,000 credits/month) but is non-commercial only; paid plans with commercial rights start at $6/month. For a live, talking agent use the WebSocket streaming endpoint, not the plain HTTP one, so audio starts as the LLM's text is still being generated; pair it with the Flash v2.5 model for low latency (about 75ms). See the real-time streaming guide.
9. Claude Design - real, launched by Anthropic Labs in April 2026. Lets you build a working prototype interface by describing it to Claude, then hand off to Claude Code to implement. Needs a paid Claude plan (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise), not the free tier.

Phase 4: Tools and channels (do this last, one connector at a time)

  1. Tools - Gmail, Calendar, Docs/Drive: official Google MCP servers exist and are free, but still labeled Developer Preview (see setup guide). Browser: Playwright MCP (Microsoft), free and open source, and its own docs say plainly it is not a security boundary on its own.
    8 (channels half). Slack: the official Slack-hosted MCP server is free. Telegram: no official MCP exists, but a maintained community wrapper around the free Bot API works (telegram-api-mcp). iMessage: no Apple API exists; you need a spare Mac running a bridge like BlueBubbles, which Hermes Agent supports directly - see its BlueBubbles setup doc.

Start this phase with the narrowest access: read-only email/calendar scopes, one channel, before adding more.

Is it safe to give an agent your email and messages?

  1. Request the narrowest scope that works (gmail.readonly, not gmail.modify or full mailbox access), never a broad scope "for later." Source: Google's Gmail scopes guidance.
  2. Give the agent its own mailbox or a forwarding address, not your everyday inbox. Sources: Agnic, LobsterMail.
  3. Require a human okay before anything irreversible goes out: an email sent, a Slack post, an iMessage. Anthropic's own guidance says to check before the action, not after. Source: Claude computer-use docs.
  4. Sandbox what the agent can run. Playwright MCP's own documentation states it is not a security boundary; the MCP project's own security guide recommends running any local connector in a container with minimal privileges. Sources: Playwright MCP, MCP security best practices.
  5. Treat anything arriving by email, web page or shared document as content that can carry hidden instructions for the agent, not just information for you. Don't let one agent hold private data access, exposure to that kind of untrusted content, and an outbound channel all at once - security researchers call that combination the "lethal trifecta," and steps 7 and 8 of this build create exactly it. Sources: Simon Willison, "The lethal trifecta", OWASP on prompt injection.

Weekend plan

Day 1: home machine, Hermes Agent, Honcho, and a brain model. Day 2: voice and interface, then add tools and channels one at a time, narrowest access first, with a human-approval step on anything that sends.

items.title: Build Your Own AI-Powered Jarvis OS 2.0 Workflow
items.hook: Learn how to build a unified AI operating system that manages your entire day.
items.summary: This guide introduces Jarvis OS 2.0, a comprehensive AI-driven workflow that integrates Claude Code, Obsidian, and local voice processing. The system uses a new classifier called Jev to route requests efficiently, significantly reducing latency and costs. By following these steps, you can create a centralized dashboard that handles tasks, research, and scheduling using markdown-based memory. It is designed to be a modular, local-first system that keeps your data and audio on your machine.

sections.heading: Overview of Jarvis OS 2.0
sections.detail: The system architecture consists of five core components: Claude Code/Codex as the engine, Obsidian as the memory vault, local voice processing (Whisper + Kokoro), Jev as the request classifier, and a dual-dashboard interface (Cockpit + HUD).

sections.heading: Jev: The Intelligent Classifier
sections.detail: Jev is a 'System One' model from TypeSafe that acts as a router rather than a text generator. It classifies voice requests into three tiers, reducing routing time from 5 seconds to under 1 second. It is highly cost-effective at $0.042 per million input tokens.

sections.heading: How the System Works
sections.detail: The workflow follows a simple loop: the user speaks or clicks in Obsidian or the HUD, Jev classifies the request, and the agent (Claude Code or Codex) executes the task, saving the output as markdown in the vault. This ensures a unified experience across different interfaces.

sections.heading: The 5 Essential Parts
sections.detail: The system requires: 1. Claude Code/Codex (engine), 2. Obsidian (memory), 3. Whisper + Kokoro (local audio), 4. Jev (classifier), and 5. Cockpit + HUD (interface).

sections.heading: Step 1: Wire the Brain
sections.detail: Users define 'skills' as individual .md files in a folder. Each dashboard button triggers a specific skill, such as 'Plan Today', 'Inbox Brief', or 'Deep Research', allowing for custom, repeatable workflows.

sections.heading: Step 2: Build the Memory
sections.detail: The vault structure is critical: /inbox for captures, /projects for WIP, /content for shipped work, and /wiki for knowledge. Every report is saved as markdown, and daily notes track the schedule and top priorities. The system uses a graph-based approach where notes and reports link together for the agent to reference.

sections.heading: Step 3: Add the Voice
sections.detail: Users can trigger the system via Ctrl+Alt+J. Local Whisper handles transcription, and Kokoro provides text-to-speech. Requests are routed into three tiers: Tier 1 (rules/data), Tier 2 (fast model), and Tier 3 (real work/terminal access).

sections.heading: Step 4: Install the Face
sections.detail: Installation is performed by cloning the 'Agentic OS V2' repository and running a specific prompt. The dashboard provides a visual interface for usage metrics, task management, and one-click workflows.

sections.heading: Call to Action

extra_sections.heading: Jev: what it actually is
extra_sections.detail:
Jev is real. It is made by TypeSafe AI, a company distinct from the unrelated same-named infrastructure company whose job listing an earlier pass mistakenly researched (now removed from this item). TypeSafe's blog describes Jev as their first "System One Model": you send it unstructured context plus a schema (the fields and fixed set of values each field can take), and it returns a typed answer with a confidence score. It classifies; it does not generate free text, matching the slide's description exactly.

Pricing claim holds up: TypeSafe's own site and docs both state $0.042 per million input tokens with output free, an exact match to the post.

Latency claim holds up: TypeSafe publishes 70-500ms end-to-end response time, well under the post's "under 1 second" figure, and consistent with the "5 seconds without Jev" comparison if the baseline is a frontier model doing the same routing job.

What did not fully check out: TypeSafe's bigger marketing numbers ("238x cheaper," "193.6x faster") are the company's own figures, not independently benchmarked, so treat those specific multipliers as a claim rather than a confirmed fact even though the base price and latency are confirmed.

Access: Jev launched September 15, 2026 as early access. Sign-up appears to be a waitlist that TypeSafe is working through progressively rather than fully open self-serve; there is no confirmed free tier. Once you have a key: an API endpoint (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone), a console for keys and a no-code playground (console.typesafe.ai), and a Python SDK (`pip install typesafe-sdk`, reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY from the environment). Jev's models (jev-1.13, jev-latest) are also listed on [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/typesafe), which is a second way in if TypeSafe's own waitlist is slow, using an OpenRouter key instead of a TypeSafe one.

If Jev access is stuck on a waitlist, the cheap alternative for pure tier-routing (not classification with typed schemas) is a small fast general model like Claude Haiku or a similarly small model, which is close to what the guide's own "Tier 2: small fast model" fallback already describes.

extra_sections.heading: Getting started: the repo and the rest of the stack
extra_sections.detail:
The "Agentic OS V2" repo is not public. It lives inside a paid membership community, Chase AI+, on Skool (roughly $98-99/month, or about $58/month billed annually per third-party listings). The creator's own blog posts about this exact build confirm it directly: the full prompt and production system are described as being "inside the Chase AI+ community." A separate free Skool tier exists with some templates and prompts, but not the repo or install prompt itself. The Instagram call to action ("Comment JARVIS") funnels into this paid community rather than handing over a free download, so this item should be treated as gated, not open, correcting an earlier read that recorded it as ungated.

The rest of the stack is public and these are the canonical sources:

1. [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/) - free note app used as the vault. Downloads for Windows, macOS, Linux, mobile.
2. [Claude Code](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) - install with `curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`, or the VS Code/JetBrains extension. Needs a Claude Pro/Max, Team, or Console account.
3. [Codex CLI](https://github.com/openai/codex) - install with `curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh` (Mac/Linux), a Windows installer, `npm install -g @openai/codex`, or `brew install --cask codex`. Needs a ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, Edu, or Enterprise account.
4. [whisper.cpp](https://github.com/ggml-org/whisper.cpp) for local speech-to-text - a dependency-free C/C++ build with no required Python/CUDA stack, GPU acceleration optional (CUDA, Vulkan, ROCm, Metal).
5. [Kokoro](https://github.com/hexgrad/kokoro) for local text-to-speech, weights on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M) - install with `pip install kokoro soundfile` plus the espeak-ng system package.

Hardware, honestly: whisper.cpp's own docs give memory by model size, from about 273MB (tiny) up to 3.9GB (large); it runs on CPU alone, no GPU required, GPU only makes it faster. For a responsive voice loop, the base or small model (under 1GB) is the realistic laptop choice. Kokoro's docs do not publish RAM or GPU minimums for inference at all, a real gap in their documentation; the only hardware figure they give is training cost, not what you need to run it. Given it is an 82M-parameter model installed with plain pip and GPU offered only as an optional flag, CPU-only operation looks like the normal path, but this is an inference from size and install method, not a documented spec. Overall: running Whisper (base/small) and Kokoro locally alongside Obsidian and a Claude Code or Codex terminal needs a few GB of free RAM beyond your OS and other apps, no dedicated GPU, and any recent Intel/AMD laptop or Apple Silicon Mac handles it; a 16GB machine is comfortable, an 8GB machine is workable but tight.

followup.next_action: If the repo is worth building, joining the paid Chase AI+ Skool community (about $98/month) is the only confirmed way to get it; the free tier and commenting "JARVIS" do not hand over the repo itself.

items.build_prompt:
# Build: excalidraw‑quick‑diagram

A tiny React app that turns a plain‑text description into an Excalidraw diagram and lets you download PNG/SVG.

I want a working repository I can push to GitHub. Build it completely -
runnable code, tests where they make sense, and a README.

## Why this matters
Shows end‑to‑end mastery: parsing natural language, generating valid Excalidraw JSON, embedding the editor, and exporting assets – a full‑stack product rather than a static tutorial clone.

## Scope
Build these:
- React front‑end with @excalidraw/excalidraw component
- Simple parser that maps keywords (flow, decision, start, end) to shapes
- Export buttons for PNG and SVG using the built‑in `exportToBlob` API
- Deployable on Vercel (no server‑side code)

Explicitly do NOT build these:
- No authentication or multi‑user collaboration
- No custom shape libraries beyond the built‑in set
- No enterprise Excalidraw+ features

## Stack - use these exact versions
- React 18
- TypeScript
- Vite
- @excalidraw/excalidraw
- TailwindCSS (optional)

## Milestones - each must be verifiably done before the next
1. **Setup project & embed editor**
   - Done when: Running React app with an empty Excalidraw canvas.
2. **Implement text‑to‑JSON parser**
   - Done when: User can type a line like "start → process → end" and see corresponding shapes appear.
3. **Add export buttons**
   - Done when: Canvas can be saved as PNG or SVG with a single click.
4. **Deploy to Vercel**
   - Done when: Public URL that works offline (PWA support).

## README must cover
- Project Overview
- Demo Screenshot / Live URL
- Tech Stack
- Installation (npm install, dev server)
- Usage (how to type descriptions, export options)
- Architecture (parser → JSON → Excalidraw component)
- Deployment (Vercel steps)
- Future Work (MCP, plugins)
- License

## Only after everything above works
- Add MCP integration so Claude can edit the diagram via API.
- Support custom colour palettes and roughness toggles.
- Persist diagrams in localStorage and allow sharing via read‑only links.

## Background
Excalidraw is an open‑source, web‑based whiteboard that lets you draw hand‑sketch‑style diagrams on an infinite canvas. It ships as a React component (npm package @excalidraw/excalidraw) that can be embedded in any web app or run as a self‑hosted instance.

## Known traps - handle these, do not rediscover them
- Every element must include the required fields (type, id, x, y, width, height) – missing any throws at export time (source).
- Arrow bindings require both startBinding/endBinding **and** the target shape’s boundElements array to be kept in sync (source).
- Do not use custom hex colours; only colours listed in color‑palette.md are accepted (source).
- Roughness > 0 gives a hand‑drawn look but can cause blurry edges; set roughness = 0 for technical diagrams (source).
- Exporting via the CLI launches Chromium; non‑finite numbers (NaN, Infinity) or stringified numbers break the renderer (source).

## Reference (checked and reachable)
- Excalidraw Developer Docs: https://docs.excalidraw.com/
- Excalidraw+ Documentation (API & MCP): https://plus.excalidraw.com/docs
- GitHub Repository: https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw
- Excalidraw developer docs: https://docs.excalidraw.com/
- https://github.com/edoardob90/excalidraw-skills/blob/main/excalidraw/gotchas.md: https://github.com/edoardob90/excalidraw-skills/blob/main/excalidraw/gotchas.md
- https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw: https://github.com/excalidraw/excalidraw
- LinkedIn Talent Solutions: https://lnkd.in/dW9cYmFv
- Excalidraw documentation | Excalidraw+ | Online whiteboard collaboration made easy: https://plus.excalidraw.com/docs
- https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXbZcV6YV8U: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXbZcV6YV8U

## How I want it delivered
- A single repository, ready to `git init` and push.
- Pin every dependency to the versions above.
- Tests that actually run. They get run before any of this is
  published, and a failure stops the whole thing.
- A README that explains what it does and how to run it, written plainly.
- No placeholder code and no TODO stubs - if something is out of scope,
  leave it out rather than stubbing it.

## How to write it

Write the way I write. A graduate student saying plainly what
something does. First person where it is natural. Short sentences. No selling.

Plain ASCII punctuation only. No em dashes, en dashes, arrows, middots, curly
quotes, bullet characters, ellipsis characters, check marks or emoji. Hyphens
and straight quotes are fine.

Never say or imply that any AI tool, model or assistant had a hand in this.
No co-author lines, no credit, no mention of one anywhere. Naming a library
the project genuinely depends on is fine.

Do not use any of these words or phrases: seamless, seamlessly, elevate, unlock, leverage, dive into, deep dive, delve, a testament to, in the realm of, it is important to note, worth noting that, furthermore, moreover, cutting edge, cutting-edge, state of the art, state-of-the-art, game changer, game-changer, best in class, best-in-class, empower, streamline, plethora, myriad, revolutionize, harness the, boasts, in today's, ever-evolving, at its core, robust and scalable, first-class, battle-tested, rock-solid, supercharge, effortlessly, in conclusion, let's explore, we'll explore, whether you're, look no further, the world of.
Do not write "not just X but Y", or "it is not X, it is Y", or "more than just".

Comments explain why something is the way it is, not what the line does. No
comment blocks five lines long, no banner headers, no restating the function
name in a docstring. If a comment would only repeat the code, leave it out.

No padding, no marketing, and no section that exists only so there is a
section.

Source this came from: https://www.instagram.com/p/DdcDA1sN8eS/?stkn=eW01N3A0ZWM3bDds

items.title: StatQuest: Understanding Word Embeddings and word2vec
items.hook: Learn how to convert words into meaningful numbers for neural networks using word embeddings and word2vec.
items.summary: Words are great for communication, but neural networks need numbers to process them. In this StatQuest, we explore how to create word embeddings by training a simple neural network to predict context. We then dive into the popular word2vec tool, which uses continuous bag-of-words and skip-gram strategies to handle large vocabularies. Finally, we explain how negative sampling makes training these massive models efficient. Bam!

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.detail: Introduction to the problem of converting words into numbers for machine learning and the goal of creating word embeddings where similar words have similar numerical values.

sections.heading: Building a Neural Network for Word Embedding
sections.detail: Step-by-step process of creating a simple neural network with inputs for unique words, activation functions representing embedding dimensions, and output layers using softmax and cross-entropy to predict the next word in a phrase.

sections.heading: Visualizing and Validating
sections.detail: Plotting word weights on a graph to visualize how backpropagation adjusts embeddings so that words used in similar contexts move closer together in vector space.

sections.heading: Summary of Main Ideas
sections.detail: Recap of how neural networks use context to optimize embeddings, making language processing easier by grouping similar words.

sections.heading: word2vec
sections.detail: Explanation of continuous bag-of-words (CBOW) and skip-gram strategies used by word2vec to capture more context than simple next-word prediction.

sections.heading: Speeding up training with Negative Sampling
sections.detail: How negative sampling improves efficiency by randomly selecting a small subset of words to avoid predicting, significantly reducing the number of weights optimized during backpropagation.

note.spoken_transcript: If you want to turn words into numbers... ...and you want those numbers to make sense... ...then use word embeddings and similar words will have similar numbers! Hooray! StatQuest! Hello, I'm Josh Starmer and welcome to StatQuest! Today we're going to talk about Word Embedding and word2vec and they're going to be clearly explained. Lightning makes using the cloud just as easy to use as your laptop and that's cool! This StatQuest is also brought to you by the letters 'A', 'B', and 'C'. 'A' always, 'B' be, 'C' curious. Always be curious! Also, I want to give a special thanks to Alex Lavaee and the students at Boston University's Spark! for letting me test this StatQuest out on them. Note: This StatQuest is focused on how neural networks can be used to create word embeddings and assumes that you are already familiar with the basic ideas of neural networks and backpropagation, as well as the main ideas about the softmax function and cross entropy. If not, check out the Quests. Words are great. We can use them to communicate all kinds of cool ideas. For example: Hey Norm, isn't StatQuest awesome? It sure is Squatch! Unfortunately, a lot of machine learning algorithms, including neural networks, don't work well with words. Hey, Neural Network, isn't StatQuest awesome! So if we want to plug words into a neural network, or some other machine learning algorithm, we need a way to turn the words into numbers. 24. 0.3 5.1 Yes, StatQuest is awesome! Bam! One super easy way to convert words into numbers is to just assign each word to a random number. For example, if someone just saw the hit movie Troll 2 and said, "Troll 2 is great!", we can just give each word a random number. Note: For the purposes of this StatQuest, were going to treat "Troll 2" as a single word. Anyway, if the next person said, "Troll 2 is awesome!", then we could reuse the random numbers that we already selected for "Troll 2" and "is", and assign a new random number to the new word, "awesome!". In theory, this is fine, but it means that even though "great!" and "awesome!" mean similar things and are used in similar ways, they have very different numbers associated with them, 4.2 and - 32.1, and that means the neural network will probably need a lot more complexity and training because learning how to correctly process the word "great!", won't help the neural network correctly use the word "awesome!". So it would be nice if similar words that are used in similar ways could be given similar numbers so that learning how to use one word will help learn how to use the other at the same time. And because the same words can be used in different contexts, or made plural, or used in some other way, it might be nice to assign each word more than one number, so that the neural network can more easily adjust to different contexts. For example, the word "great" can be used in a positive way, like "StatQuest is great!", and it can also be used in a sarcastic, negative way, like "My cell phone is broken, great", and it would be nice if we had one number that could keep track of the positive ways that "great" is used and a different number to keep track of the negative ways. Hey Josh, deciding what words are similar and used in similar contexts sounds like a lot of work. And using more than one number per word to account for different contexts sounds like even more work. Don't worry Squatch. The good news is that we can get a super simple neural network to do all of the work for us. Bam! To show how we can get a super simple neural network to figure out what numbers should go with different words. Let's imagine we have two phrases: "Troll 2 is great!" and "Gymkata is great!". Anyway, both phrases have two words, "Troll 2" and "Gymkata", in similar contexts, because someone, and I'm not going to name names, thinks that these two terrible movies are great! So, in order to create a neural network to figure out what numbers we should associate with each word, the first thing we do is create inputs for each unique word. In this case, we have four unique words in the training data, so we have four inputs. Now we connect each input to at least one activation function. Note: This activation function uses the identity function, and thus, the input value is the same as the output value. In other words, this activation function doesn't do anything except give us a place to do addition. The number of activation functions corresponds to how many numbers we want to associate with each word. And the weights on those connections will ultimately be the numbers that we associate with each word. Now, in this example, we want to associate two numbers with each word. So that means we'll use two activation functions. And the weights on the connections to the second activation function will be another number associated with each word. However, like always, these weights start out with random values that we will optimize with backpropagation. Now, in order to do backpropagation, we have to make predictions. So we'll use the input word to predict the next word in the phrase. So if the phrase is "Troll 2 is great", then we can use the word "Troll 2" to predict the word "is". In other words, if the input word is "Troll 2", and we indicate that by putting a 1 into the "Troll 2" input and 0s into all of the other inputs, then we want the output for the word, "is", to have the largest value. And if the input word is "is", which means that the input for "is" is is 1 and all of the other inputs are 0, then we want the output for the next word, "great!", to have the largest value. Lastly, if the input word is "Gymkata", which means that the input for "Gymkata" is 1 and all of the other inputs are 0, then we want the output for the next word, "is", to have the largest value. In order to make these predictions, we connect the activation functions to outputs and we add weights to those connections with random initialization values. And then we run the outputs through the softmax function because we have multiple outputs for classification. And that means we can use the cross entropy loss function for backpropagation. Again, the goal is to train this neural network so that it correctly predicts the next word in a phrase. And now, before training, if we plug the word "Troll 2" into the input and do the math, we get lucky and correctly predict the next word, "is", but just barely. However, when we plug the word "is" into the input and do the math, then we fail to correctly predict the next word "great!" and instead predict "is". So we need to train this neural network. However, before we optimize all of the weights, remember that I said that these weights would be the numbers associated with each word. And since, in this example, we have two weights for each word, we can plot each word on a graph that has the weight values to the top activation function on the x axis and the weight values the bottom activation function on the y-axis. For example, the word "Troll 2" goes here, because it's top weight is 0.38 and its bottom weight is 0.42. Likewise, the word "is" goes here, and the word "great" goes here, and "Gymkata" goes here. Now, with this graph, we see that the words "Troll 2" and "Gymkata" are currently no more similar to each other as they are to any of the other words. However, because both words appear in the same context in the training data, we hope that backpropagation will make their weights more similar. So we start with these weights and we end up with these new weights. The new weights on the connections from the inputs to the activation functions are the word embeddings. And when we plot the words using the new weights, which are now the embeddings, we see that "Troll 2" and "Gymkata" are now relatively close to each other compared to the other words in the training data. Bam! Now that we've trained the neural network, we can see how well it predicts the next word. For example, if we plug the word "Troll 2" into the input and do the math, then the output for the next word, "is", is 1 and everything else is 0, and that is exactly what we wanted. And when we plug the word "is" into the input and do the math, then the output for the next word in both phrases "great!" is 1 and everything else is 0. Lastly, when we plug the word "Gymkata" into the input and do the math, then the output for the next word, "is", is 1 and everything else is 0. Bam! Now, before we talk about a popular word embedding tool, word2vec, let's summarize what we've learned so far. First, rather than just assign random numbers to words, we can train a relatively simple neural network to assign numbers for us. The advantage of using a neural network is that it can use the context of words in the training data set to optimize weights that can be used for the embeddings. And this can result in similar words ending up with similar embeddings. Lastly, having similar words with similar embeddings means training a neural network to process language is easier because learning how one word is used helps learn how similar words are used. Double bam! Now, so far, we've shown we can train a neural network to predict the next word in each phrase. But just predicting the next word doesn't give us a lot of context to understand each one. So now let's learn about the two strategies that word2vec, a popular method for creating word embeddings, uses to include more context. The first method, called "continuous bag-of-words", increases the context by using the surrounding words to predict what occurs in the middle. For example, the continuous bag-of-words method could use the words "Troll 2" and "great!" to predict the word that occurs between them, "is". The second method, called "skip-gram", increases the context by using the word in the middle to predict the surrounding words. For example, the skip-gram method could use the word "is" to predict the surrounding words "Troll 2", "great!" and "Gymkata". Lastly, before we're done, just know that in practice, instead of using just 2 activation functions to create 2 embeddings per word, people often use 100 or more activation functions to create a lot of embeddings per word. And instead of using 2 sentences for training, they use the entire wikipedia. Thus, instead of just having a vocabulary of 4 words and phrases, word2vec might have a vocabulary of about 3 million words and phrases. Thus, the total number of weights in this neural network that we need to optimize is 3 million words and phrases times at least 100, the number of weights each word has going to the activation functions, x 2, for the weights that get us from the activation functions to the outputs, for a total of 600 million weights. So training can be slow. However, one way that word2vec speeds things up is to use something called Negative Sampling. Negative sampling works by randomly selecting a subset of words we don't want to predict for optimization. For example, say like we wanted the word "aardvark" to predict the word "a". That means that only the word "aardvark" has a 1 in it and all of the other words have zeros, and that means we can ignore the weights coming from every word but "aardvark", because the other words multiply their weights by zero. That alone removes close to 300 million weights from this optimization step. However, we still have 300 million weights after the activation functions. So, because we want to predict the word "a", then we don't want to predict "aardvark", "abandon", and all of the other words. So for this example, let's imagine word2vec randomly selects "abandon" as a word we don't want to predict. Note: In practice, word2vec would select between 2 and 20 words that we don't want to predict. However, in this example, we just select one, "abandon". So now word2vec only uses the output values for "a" and "abandon", and that means for this round of backpropagation, we can ignore the weights that lead to all of the other possible outputs. So, in the end, out of the 600 million total weights in this neural network, we only optimize 300 per step. And this is one way that word2vec can efficiently create lots of word embeddings for each word in a large vocabulary. Triple bam! Now it's time for some shameless self-promotion. If you want to review statistics and machine learning offline, check out the StatQuest PDF study guides and my book, The StatQuest Illustrated Guide to Machine Learning at statquest.org. There's something for everyone. Hooray! We've made it to the end of another exciting StatQuest. If you liked this StatQuest and want to see more, please subscribe. And if you want to support StatQuest, consider contributing to my patreon campaign, becoming a channel member, buying one or two of my original songs, or a t-shirt, or a hoodie, or just donate, the links are in the description below. All right until next time Quest on!

items.title: A Light Introduction to Large Language Models and Transformers
items.hook: Understand the mathematical mechanics behind how chatbots predict text and learn language.
items.summary: This video provides a conceptual overview of how large language models function, from the basic premise of word prediction to the complex architecture of transformers. I explain how models are trained on vast amounts of internet text to tune billions of parameters, and how reinforcement learning with human feedback refines their behavior. We also explore the role of GPUs in parallel processing and the specific mechanisms of attention and feed-forward networks. Ultimately, these models are sophisticated mathematical functions that produce emergent, fluent text through probabilistic prediction.

sections.heading: The Chatbot Mechanism
sections.detail: Explains chatbots as systems that predict the next word in a sequence by assigning probabilities to all possible words, treating the interaction as a completion of a script.

sections.heading: Training and Parameters
sections.detail: Describes pre-training as tuning billions of weights using backpropagation on massive text datasets to improve prediction accuracy.

sections.heading: Computational Scale
sections.detail: Highlights the immense computational cost of training, noting it would take over 100 million years to perform the necessary operations at a rate of one billion per second.

sections.heading: Refinement and Transformers
sections.detail: Covers reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) and the shift from sequential processing to the parallel architecture of transformers using attention and feed-forward networks.

sections.heading: Emergent Behavior
sections.detail: Concludes that while the framework is designed by researchers, the specific output behavior is an emergent phenomenon resulting from the tuned parameters.

sections.heading: The Mechanism of Chatbots
sections.detail: Chatbots function by predicting the next word in a sequence. They treat a conversation as a script where the AI's response is missing, using a mathematical function to assign probabilities to all possible next words.

sections.heading: Reinforcement Learning
sections.detail: Beyond pre-training, models undergo reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) to align their outputs with user preferences and improve helpfulness.

sections.heading: Transformer Architecture
sections.detail: Transformers process text in parallel rather than sequentially. They use 'attention' to allow words to influence each other's meanings based on context, and feed-forward networks to store learned patterns.

note.spoken_transcript: Imagine you happen across a short movie script that describes a scene between a person and their AI assistant. The script has what the person asks the AI, but the AI's response has been torn off. Suppose you also have this powerful magical machine that can take any text and provide a sensible prediction of what word comes next. You could then finish the script by feeding in what you have to the machine, seeing what it would predict to start the AI's answer, and then repeating this over and over with a growing script completing the dialogue. When you interact with a chatbot, this is exactly what's happening. A large language model is a sophisticated mathematical function that predicts what word comes next for any piece of text. Instead of predicting one word with certainty, though, what it does is assign a probability to all possible next words. To build a chatbot, what you do is lay out some text that describes an interaction between a user and a hypothetical AI assistant, you add on whatever the user types in as the first part of the interaction, and then have the model repeatedly predict the next word that such a hypothetical AI assistant would say in response, and that's what's presented to the user. In doing this, the output tends to look a lot more natural if you allow it to select less likely words along the way at random. So what this means is even though the model itself is deterministic, a given prompt typically gives a different answer each time it's run. Models learn how to make these predictions by processing an enormous amount of text, typically pulled from the internet. For a standard human to read the amount of text that was used to train GPT-3, for example, if they read non-stop 24-7, it would take over 2600 years. Larger models since then train on much, much more. You can think of training a little bit like tuning the dials on a big machine. The way that a language model behaves is entirely determined by these many different continuous values, usually called parameters or weights. Changing those parameters will change the probabilities that the model gives for the next word on a given input. What puts the large in large language model is how they can have hundreds of billions of these parameters. No human ever deliberately sets those parameters. Instead, they begin at random, meaning the model just outputs gibberish, but they're repeatedly refined based on many example pieces of text. One of these training examples could be just a handful of words, or it could be thousands, but in either case, the way this works is to pass in all but the last word from that example into the model and compare the prediction that it makes with the true last word from the example. An algorithm called backpropagation is used to tweak all of the parameters in such a way that it makes the model a little more likely to choose the true last word and a little less likely to choose all the others. When you do this for many, many trillions of examples, not only does the model start to give more accurate predictions on the training data, but it also starts to make more reasonable predictions on text that it's never seen before. Given the huge number of parameters and the enormous amount of training data, the scale of computation involved in training a large language model is mind-boggling. To illustrate, imagine that you could perform one billion additions and multiplications every single second. How long do you think it would take for you to do all of the operations involved in training the largest language models? Do you think it would take a year? Maybe something like 10,000 years? The answer is actually much more than that. It's well over 100 million years. This is only part of the story, though. This whole process is called pre-training. The goal of auto-completing a random passage of text from the internet is very different from the goal of being a good AI assistant. To address this, chatbots undergo another type of training, just as important, called reinforcement learning with human feedback. Workers flag unhelpful or problematic predictions, and their corrections further change the model's parameters, making them more likely to give predictions that users prefer. Looking back at the pre-training, though, this staggering amount of computation is only made possible by using special computer chips that are optimized for running many operations in parallel, known as GPUs. However, not all language models can be easily parallelized. Prior to 2017, most language models would process text one word at a time, but then a team of researchers at Google introduced a new model known as the transformer. Transformers don't read text from the start to the finish, they soak it all in at once, in parallel. The very first step inside a transformer, and most other language models for that matter, is to associate each word with a long list of numbers. The reason for this is that the training process only works with continuous values, so you have to somehow encode language using numbers, and each of these lists of numbers may somehow encode the meaning of the corresponding word. What makes transformers unique is their reliance on a special operation known as attention. This operation gives all of these lists of numbers a chance to talk to one another and refine the meanings they encode based on the context around, all done in parallel. For example, the numbers encoding the word bank might be changed based on the context surrounding it to somehow encode the more specific notion of a riverbank. Transformers typically also include a second type of operation known as a feed-forward neural network, and this gives the model extra capacity to store more patterns about language learned during training. All of this data repeatedly flows through many different iterations of these two fundamental operations, and as it does so, the hope is that each list of numbers is enriched to encode whatever information might be needed to make an accurate prediction of what word follows in the passage. At the end, one final function is performed on the last vector in this sequence, which now has had a chance to be influenced by all the other context from the input text, as well as everything the model learned during training, to produce a prediction of the next word. Again, the model's prediction looks like a probability for every possible next word. Although researchers design the framework for how each of these steps work, it's important to understand that the specific behavior is an emergent phenomenon based on how those hundreds of billions of parameters are tuned during training. This makes it incredibly challenging to determine why the model makes the exact predictions that it does. What you can see is that when you use large language model predictions to autocomplete a prompt, the words that it generates are uncannily fluent, fascinating, and even useful. If you're a new viewer and you're curious about more details on how transformers and attention work, boy do I have some material for you. One option is to jump into a series I made about deep learning, where we visualize and motivate the details of attention and all the other steps in a transformer. Also, on my second channel I just posted a talk I gave a couple months ago about this topic for the company TNG in Munich. Sometimes I actually prefer the content I make as a casual talk rather than a produced video, but I leave it up to you which one of these feels like the better follow-on.

onscreen_text: WHY TRANSFORMER IS IMPORTANT IN AI?
Used in Text, Vision, Speech & Multimodal AI
What is the intuition behind the self-attention mechanism in Transformers? How does it help in capturing long-range dependencies?
Self-attention allows each token to attend to all other tokens in the input sequence and compute a weighted representation.
It uses Query (Q), Key (K) and Value (V) vectors to calculate attention scores.
The attention score between two tokens is based on the similarity of their Q and K vectors. If two tokens are similar, the model gives them more weight.
This helps in capturing long-range dependencies because tokens far apart in the sequence can still have high similarity.
Unlike RNNs/CNNs, self-attention is parallelizable and more efficient for long sequences.
Be clear about the role of Q, K, V and why scaling is required (to avoid large dot products).
Attention (QK^T / sqrt(d_k)) -> Softmax -> Output (n x d_model)
Attention (Q, K, V) = softmax((QK^T) / sqrt(d_k)) V
Scaling by sqrt(d_k) prevents large dot products.
Multi-head attention uses multiple heads to attend to information from different representation subspaces.
Explain the difference between encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder Transformer architectures. Give one example of each.
Encoder-only: Used for understanding tasks (e.g., classification, sentence embedding). It only has an encoder stack.
Decoder-only: Used for generation tasks (e.g., language modeling). It only has a decoder stack with causal masking.
Encoder-Decoder: Used for sequence-to-sequence tasks (e.g., translation, summarization). It has both encoder and decoder stacks with cross-attention.
Why does BERT use bidirectional attention while GPT uses causal masking?
What is positional encoding in Transformers? Discuss different types of positional encoding and why it is needed.

enrich.what_it_is: LangGraph is a low-level orchestration runtime and framework for building stateful, multi-actor LLM applications using graph architectures [1][4]. Inspired by Google's Pregel system, it coordinates agents and deterministic code as nodes connected by edges, executing in discrete super-steps with explicit message-passing [1][4]. It provides native persistence, cyclical execution loops, and first-class human-in-the-loop controls without abstracting away model prompts or code [1][4].
enrich.current_state: The latest stable release in the repository is langgraph 1.2.12 (with langgraph-sdk 0.4.5 and langgraph-checkpoint 4.2.0) [5]; the exact release date is not explicitly stated in the release index [5]. The saved post's core concepts—nodes, edges, StateGraph, memory/persistence, human-in-the-loop, and tool calling—remain accurate and foundational to the framework [1][3][4].
enrich.why_it_matters: Unlike standard DAG workflow tools or rigid black-box agent frameworks, LangGraph allows arbitrary cyclical loops and enables mixing deterministic, hand-coded business logic with agentic LLM steps in a single execution graph [1]. It unlocks durable execution through checkpointers that save state snapshots at every super-step, enabling fault tolerance, time-travel debugging, and native pause-and-resume human-in-the-loop workflows via interrupt() [1][4].
prerequisites: Intermediate Python (async programming, type annotations, and TypedDict / Pydantic schemas) [3][4]
Basic understanding of LLM tool calling / function calling patterns [3]
Foundational graph theory concepts (nodes, directed edges, conditional routing, cycles) [3][4]

gotchas: State overwriting: Failing to use channel reducers like Annotated[list[AnyMessage], operator.add] causes nodes to overwrite the message history instead of appending to it [3][4].
Missing compilation: Forgetting to call .compile() on the StateGraph builder before attempting to invoke or stream executions [3].
Infinite loops in conditional edges: Not configuring a clean base case or terminal condition routing to END in conditional routing functions [3][4].

Confusing the Graph API with the Functional API: LangGraph supports both StateGraph (Graph API) and function-based workflows (Functional API); mixing mental models can cause state synchronization bugs [3][4].
beyond_the_post: Dual APIs: LangGraph provides both a Graph API (StateGraph) and a Functional API for single-function workflows [3][4].
Modern Checkpointer Ecosystem: Production checkpointing packages such as langgraph-checkpoint-postgres and delta channel history optimizations [5].
Schema-enforced Interrupts: Recent support for structured responses using response_schema directly inside interrupt() calls [5].
LangSmith Integration: Automated trace evaluation and observability via LangSmith Engine [1][2][3].

## Background
LangGraph is a low-level orchestration runtime and framework for building stateful, multi-actor LLM applications using graph architectures. Inspired by Google's Pregel system, it coordinates agents and deterministic code as nodes connected by edges, executing in discrete super-steps with explicit message-passing. It provides native persistence, cyclical execution loops, and first-class human-in-the-loop controls without abstracting away model prompts or code.

## Known traps - handle these, do not rediscover them
- State overwriting: Failing to use channel reducers like Annotated[list[AnyMessage], operator.add] causes nodes to overwrite the message history instead of appending to it.
- Missing compilation: Forgetting to call .compile() on the StateGraph builder before attempting to invoke or stream executions.
- Infinite loops in conditional edges: Not configuring a clean base case or terminal condition routing to END in conditional routing functions.
- Confusing the Graph API with the Functional API: LangGraph supports both StateGraph (Graph API) and function-based workflows (Functional API); mixing mental models can cause state synchronization bugs.
